summaries.example: Imagine wearing glasses that make every object look blue. You can still learn where the objects are, but what you see is shaped by the glasses. Some philosophers called idealists ask a similar question: how much of the world we know is shaped by the mind? Berkeley went further, arguing that things are ideas perceived by minds, including a divine mind. Kant offered a different view: our experience has forms, such as space and time, supplied by our minds, while things may still exist independently of us.
summaries.summary: Idealism is not one single idea. In everyday speech, an idealist may be an hopeful person, but in philosophy the word usually concerns the relation between mind and reality. Some idealists say that minds, ideas, or spirit are the deepest kind of reality. Others begin with knowledge: we never encounter the world without using mental abilities that organize what we experience. Berkeley argued that ideas exist only when perceived and that bodies depend on minds, including God’s mind. Hume used experience and habit to explain beliefs about causes, selves, and objects, but his position remains difficult to classify. Kant argued that space and time belong to the way human beings experience things, while things independent of our experience may still exist. German idealists such as Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel developed more active views in which self-consciousness, thinking, and the relation between subject and object help explain reality. Schopenhauer connected the world behind appearances with a non-rational will, while Nietzsche criticized idealism yet explored how perspectives and interpretations shape knowledge. British and American idealists later defended mental or spiritual accounts of reality, before critics such as Moore and Russell challenged them. The history shows that idealism is a family of changing answers to questions about minds, knowledge, and what is real.
key_ideas: Idealism has several forms, so its meaning depends on the philosopher and the question being asked.
Some idealists argue that reality itself is mental. Others argue that our knowledge of reality is always shaped by the mind.
Berkeley made ideas and minds central to reality, while Hume questioned how far we can know about minds and outside objects.
Kant said space and time are forms through which human beings experience things. He still allowed that things exist independently of our representations.
Later German idealists focused on activity, self-consciousness, and the connection between thinking and being.
The entry follows idealism from early modern philosophy through German, British, and American versions, and then its decline and later defenses.
summaries.why_it_matters: Idealism asks a question that appears in ordinary life: do we discover the world exactly as it is, or does the mind help shape what we experience and understand? Thinking about this can make us more careful about the difference between what seems true, what we can know, and what may exist beyond our viewpoint. It also helps explain why philosophers can agree about experience while disagreeing about reality.

important_terms.definition: A family of philosophical views that gives the mental—such as ideas, thought, spirit, or experience—a very important place in explaining reality.
The view that reality is made up only of minds and what minds experience or think.
A view about how knowing works: what we know is shaped by the ways our minds organize experience.
The belief that some things exist independently of minds and experiences.
Berkeley’s name for his view that bodies do not exist as mind-independent material substances, although minds and ideas do exist.

questions_to_think_about: If everything you see is seen through your mind, does that mean the outside world is only an idea?
Can something be real even if you cannot know exactly what it is like?
How might two people’s points of view affect what they think is true?
Is a person better understood as a thinking mind, a body, or both?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether the mind creates order or discovers it?

summaries.example: Suppose a scientist studies a physical object using measurements arranged in space and time. Kant’s position suggests that spatial and temporal organization is not simply copied from things as they are independently of us; it is also supplied by the forms through which human sensibility experiences objects. This does not make the object unreal. Kant combines transcendental idealism—the claim that space and time are necessary features of human representation—with empirical realism about ordinary objects. By contrast, Berkeley argues more radically that an unperceived material object is incoherent, while Hegel treats the opposition between thought and being as something philosophy must work to
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents idealism as a historically varied family of positions rather than a single doctrine. A useful organizing distinction concerns the route taken to an idealist conclusion. Metaphysical arguments begin with constraints on what can exist and claim that only minds, ideas, spirit, or activity satisfy them. Epistemological arguments begin with the conditions of knowledge and claim that the known must be structurally related to knowing in a necessary way. These routes may be combined, as in Berkeley, or separated, as in some later idealists. Early modern debates supplied the main problems. Rationalists considered mind, substance, God, and the structure of reality, while British philosophers emphasized the origin and limits of knowledge. Locke remained agnostic about the ultimate nature of material and spiritual substance. Berkeley argued that if ideas are the immediate objects of knowledge, mind-independent matter cannot be coherently retained; his immaterialism is intended to preserve a realistic world of perceived bodies and minds rather than collapse into skepticism. Hume explained causal necessity through custom, imagination, and felt transitions among perceptions. His account of the self and external objects as constructed from perceptions creates a tension between natural belief, skepticism, and idealism. Kant’s transcendental idealism is more qualified. He argues that space and time are forms of intuition and that categories such as causation organize experience. Since a priori knowledge requires necessary correspondence, these forms cannot simply be properties of things in themselves. Yet Kant maintains that objects independent of representations exist, so his view is also empirically realist and theoretically agnostic about their ultimate nature.᠎
key_ideas: The entry recommends distinguishing metaphysical arguments for idealism from epistemological arguments, rather than treating idealism simply as a theory of knowledge.
Berkeley moves from the claim that ideas are the immediate objects of knowledge toward the conclusion that bodies must be ideas in minds, with divine perception supporting the stability of the world.
Hume relocates necessary connection in causation to habits and impressions in the mind. His views can appear idealist, skeptical, naturalist, or agnostic depending on interpretation.

Kant argues that a priori knowledge of geometry and time cannot describe things in themselves unless the necessary structure comes from our own forms of intuition. He nevertheless defends the existence of objects independent of representations.

Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel transform idealism into a dynamic account of activity, self-consciousness, and the subject-object relation. Hegel rejects a simple choice between idealism and realism and argues for the fundamental reality of thinking.

Schopenhauer identifies the reality behind appearances with will, Nietzsche criticizes metaphysical idealism while developing perspectival themes, and British and American idealists revive spiritual or mental accounts before twentieth-century realists challenge them.
summaries.why_it_matters: Idealism matters because it forces philosophy to separate three questions that are easily blended: what exists, how we know it, and how our conceptual or perceptual powers shape what appears. The history also shows that “mind-dependent” need not mean “dependent on my private imagination.” Berkeley appeals to divine mind; German idealists emphasize activity or thought; British idealists invoke a larger intelligence; and Hegel seeks a framework in which the opposition between idealism and realism is itself overcome. Studying these alternatives clarifies both the strengths and limits of claims about objectivity, perspective, freedom, science, and reality.

important_terms.definition: A broad family of views that gives ontological priority to the mental, conceptual, ideational, or spiritual over the non-mental.
An argument from claims about existence: it identifies conditions anything real must satisfy and argues that only minds or mental realities satisfy them.
An argument from claims about knowledge: it argues that what can be known must share a necessary structural relation with knowing, and therefore must be mental in some relevant sense.
Kant’s view that space and time are necessary forms of human sensibility and characterize appearances, not things as they are independently of our representations.
Kant’s claim that ordinary objects of experience are real, even though their ultimate, non-spatiotemporal nature cannot be theoretically known.
A view that things exist independently of our representations or minds. The entry distinguishes several kinds of realism rather than treating the term as having one fixed meaning.
Berkeley’s position that ideas are passive contents of perception and that bodies are not mind-independent material substances; minds remain active perceivers.
A philosophical position treating reality as one fundamental whole rather than as ultimately composed of independent kinds of substance.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that knowledge is always from a point of view entail that reality itself is mind-dependent?
Is Kant’s combination of transcendental idealism and empirical realism stable, or does it leave a tension between appearances and things in themselves?
Does Berkeley’s argument confuse conceiving an unperceived object with the object’s being unperceived?
Can a theory make mind fundamental without reducing everything to an individual human mind?
When Hegel says thinking and being are ultimately identical, is this a metaphysical claim, an epistemological claim, or both?

summaries.example: Think about a video game. The game’s world has objects, rules, and locations, but players can experience it only through the screen and the game’s controls. One philosopher might say the world is made of experiences in a mind. Another might say the game world exists, but the player’s equipment determines how it appears. Berkeley’s view is closer to the first idea: objects are ideas perceived by minds. Kant’s view is closer to the second: our minds contribute forms such as space and time, but objects can still be real beyond our particular experience.
summaries.summary: Philosophical idealism is a family of views about the place of mind in reality and knowledge. Some idealists claim that minds, ideas, or spirit are the ultimate reality. Others begin with a problem about knowledge: everything we know is organized through perception, thought, language, or concepts, so perhaps what we know cannot be separated from the mind’s contribution. The entry follows these ideas from early modern philosophy to the twentieth century. Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, and Malebranche helped shape questions about mind, body, God, substance, and knowledge, although they did not all call themselves idealists. Locke argued that we know ideas while remaining unsure about the hidden nature of substances. Berkeley rejected this uncertainty, arguing that bodies are collections of ideas perceived by minds and that a divine mind explains their continued existence. Hume used impressions, ideas, custom, and imagination to explain belief. His account of the self and outside objects leaves an unresolved tension between ordinary belief and philosophical doubt. Kant developed transcendental idealism. He claimed that space and time are forms through which humans experience objects, while things independent of our representations may still exist. Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel developed more active versions, emphasizing self-consciousness, activity, and the connection between thinking and being. Schopenhauer described the underlying reality as will. Nietzsche attacked idealism as a flight from changing reality but also explored how perspectives and interpretation influence knowledge. British and American idealism later made mind or spirit central to metaphysics, ethics, and social thought, before Moore, Russell, and other realists challenged it.
key_ideas: The word idealism can mean different things in everyday life and in philosophy, and philosophers use it in several different ways.
Berkeley argues that ideas are what minds perceive and that unperceived material substance cannot be meaningfully separated from ideas.
Hume explains many beliefs through custom and imagination, but scholars disagree about whether his position is mainly skeptical, naturalistic, or partly idealist.
Kant says our minds organize experience through space, time, and basic concepts. He does not simply deny that things exist outside our minds.
German idealists make the mind active: reality is connected with self-conscious activity, thought, or the developing relation between subject and object.
Later idealism appeared in Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and British and American philosophy, but it faced strong criticism from twentieth-century realists.
summaries.why_it_matters: Idealism matters because it makes us examine assumptions we often overlook. When we see a tree, are we directly grasping the tree as it is, or are we receiving an experience shaped by our senses and concepts? The philosophers in this tradition give different answers. Comparing them helps us distinguish appearance from reality, personal viewpoint from shared knowledge, and uncertainty from skepticism. It also shows why questions about knowledge can lead to larger questions about what exists.

important_terms.definition: A group of theories that gives minds, ideas, spirit, reason, or thought a basic role in explaining what is real.
An idealist view claiming that reality itself is ultimately mental or spiritual, rather than made of mind-independent matter alone.
An argument saying that because human knowledge is shaped by mental activity, what is known must have a necessary relation to the mind.
The view that at least some things exist independently of what anyone thinks or experiences.
The name Berkeley used for his claim that material bodies do not exist independently of minds, though minds and ideas do exist.
Kant’s view that space and time are forms supplied by human sensibility, while ordinary objects can still be empirically real.
A theory saying that reality is fundamentally one rather than made from independently existing kinds of substance.

questions_to_think_about: If all your experiences are mental, does it follow that the things you experience are only mental?
Why might someone prefer to remain uncertain about what matter or mind is ultimately made of?
Can our minds shape knowledge without inventing the whole world?
What is the difference between saying that reality is one and saying that everything is made of matter?
Why might a philosopher connect idealism with freedom or moral responsibility?
